name: Tea tree oil

lead: Tea tree oil is the essential oil distilled from the leaves of Melaleuca alternifolia, a tree native to eastern Australia. It is used in soaps, washes, gels and shampoos for acne, fungal skin conditions, body odor and eyelid cleansing.

In laboratory studies it has broad antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity. Human evidence is a mix of small pilot trials (for example, a 5% acne gel pilot with 18 people) and eyelid-mite studies; large trials for appearance outcomes are scarce.

paras: Its main component, terpinen-4-ol, disrupts the membranes of bacteria and yeast in laboratory studies, and has been shown to suppress inflammatory mediators such as TNF-alpha and interleukins in activated human monocytes.

Reviews and dermatology references note irritation and allergic contact dermatitis; an encyclopedic summary reports reactions in a small percentage of users and toxicity if swallowed. Product labels advise external use only. Pure oil is generally used diluted.

lead: Tea tree oil is an essential oil produced by steam distillation of Melaleuca alternifolia leaves, a plant native to eastern Australia, with terpinen-4-ol as its primary active component [1]. A 2006 review describes it as used for almost 100 years in Australia and now sold worldwide as neat oil and as an ingredient in many products, chiefly for its antiseptic and anti-inflammatory properties [2].

Laboratory studies show broad antimicrobial activity against bacteria, yeast and fungi, and anti-inflammatory effects on human monocytes [3][4][5][6]. Human trials include a pilot study of tea tree oil gel for acne, studies of its use against Demodex mites and blepharitis, and trials in oral care and wound-related uses [7][8][9][10].
Its main role in looksmaxxing-type contexts is as an acne and skin-care ingredient; forum mentions are sparse. Contact allergy and toxicity on ingestion are documented [11][1].
infobox: From the 1920s for antiseptic use, per an encyclopedic summary [1]

paras: A US label for a tea tree oil antifungal soap lists use against athlete's foot, jock itch and ringworm, and says it helps reduce body odor, acne, itching and eczema from fungi [12]. A systematic review of cosmeceuticals for photoaging included tea tree oil among botanicals searched [13].
One T Nation user describes making a shave gel from tea tree oil, witch hazel and aloe to avoid post-shave breakouts [14].

Tea tree oil has been studied for eyelid Demodex infestation and blepharitis, including 5% tea tree oil as a comparator to intense pulsed light, an eye gel trial in anterior blepharitis and eyelid cleansers [8][15][16][9][17][18]. Other studies and registrations cover MRSA decolonization body wash, hand-hygiene soap, nasal use in dialysis patients, burns, nipple cracks and dental or periodontal applications [19][20][21][22][23][24][10][25].

In laboratory studies, exposure to tea tree oil damaged cell membranes of Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus and Candida albicans [3], and time-kill and leakage assays on S. aureus attributed activity to components including terpinen-4-ol, 1,8-cineole and alpha-terpineol [4][26]. Terpinen-4-ol suppressed production of TNF-alpha, interleukins and prostaglandin E2 by activated human monocytes [6]. Antifungal activity of its components has also been reported [5].

A registered phase II pilot of tea tree oil gel for facial acne enrolled 18 participants [7]; an encyclopedic summary states that 5% gels have shown efficacy comparable to benzoyl peroxide, though the published literature do not include the underlying trial data [1].

In ophthalmology, a randomized study of 40 patients compared intense pulsed light with 5% tea tree oil as the control for ocular demodicosis [8]. An open-label trial compared tea tree oil eye gel with standard treatment in anterior blepharitis [15]. A randomized crossover study of five commercial anti-demodectic eyelid cleansers assessed short-term tolerability in 30 healthy people [16]. Registered trials involve chronic blepharitis (n=34), ocular demodicosis (n=60) and dry eye compared with azithromycin (n=50) [9][17][18].

A protocol for a randomized trial of 5% tea tree oil body wash against standard body wash to prevent MRSA colonization in critically ill adults has been published [19]. A randomized trial examined a tea tree oil soap for hand hygiene [20]. Small registered studies cover burns (n=30), nipple cracks (n=90) and gum disease [22][23][10][24].
The published literature contain no large randomized trial of tea tree oil for facial appearance, wrinkles or hair growth.

A dermatology reference on tea tree oil covers allergic contact dermatitis [11], and a 2005 review in Cutis discusses its use and tolerability [27]. An encyclopedic summary reports that diluted tea tree oil is generally well tolerated, with irritation, dryness or allergic contact dermatitis in a small percentage of users, and that undiluted use can cause severe irritation and ingestion can be toxic [1]. That summary is AI-generated. Product labelling advises external use only [12]. A 2006 review notes that the toxicity of the oil is discussed briefly in the literature [2].

On T Nation, tea tree oil appears in passing, including the shave-gel recipe above [14]. One poster stated that there is research suggesting lavender and tea tree oil lower testosterone [28]; the published literature contain no study of this.
